steps.title: Calculate surfactant amounts
steps.instruction: Choose a surfactant concentration (e.g., 75 mM or 150 mM) and compute the masses for a 50:50 mol % natural lipid : DPC mixture; for GPx4 use 6.6 mg DPC (MW 351.462 g·mol⁻¹) and 11.6 mg DLPC (MW 621.826 g·mol⁻¹) or 12.1 mg soy lecithin (or porcine brain or bovine heart lipids). Record the water‑loading target W₀ (e.g., W₀ = 20 corresponds to 13.5 µL water in a 500 µL total sample).

steps.title: Prepare protein for encapsulation
steps.instruction: Select either concentration‑based or vacuum‑concentration/lyophilization preparation and follow the corresponding workflow.

substeps.instruction: Concentration method: Verify the starting protein solution is ≥1.2 mg·mL⁻¹ by Bradford assay. Using a 1.5 mL spin concentrator with a 10 kDa PES membrane, concentrate the protein directly to the volume required for the chosen W₀ (e.g., ~13.5 µL water plus protein). Perform at 4 °C or room temperature as appropriate for the protein.

Vacuum‑concentration method (performed the day before): Buffer‑exchange the protein into dilute protein buffer (see step “Make dilute protein buffer”). Prepare 60 mL dilute buffer, add 1 mL of 1.2 mg·mL⁻¹ protein, and concentrate in a 10 kDa PES spin concentrator (20 mL capacity) at 3 260 × g until the volume reaches 500 µL. Repeat the buffer‑exchange two more times (add 20 mL buffer, centrifuge to 500 µL, repeat). Transfer the final 500 µL to a 1.5 mL glass vial, freeze at –80 °C for ≥10 min, then place in a speed‑vacuum overnight to sublimate solvent, leaving only protein and dilute buffer components.
Note: Account for up to 2‑fold protein loss during buffer exchange by loading excess protein initially.

steps.title: Remove metal from soy lecithin
steps.instruction: In a fume hood, dry chloroform (10 mL) and methanol (5 mL) over sodium sulfate overnight, then decant the dried solvents. Prepare 15 mL of this mobile phase, weigh 1.0 g soy lecithin into a 20 mL scintillation vial, add the mobile phase and stir until dissolved. Add 5 mL of 200 mM EDTA (pH 6.0) and stir 24 h with a sealed lid and parafilm. Transfer the mixture to a separatory funnel, shake, vent, and allow phases to separate. Collect the bottom organic layer into a graduated cylinder, bring the volume to 15 mL with fresh mobile phase, and transfer to a clean 20 mL scintillation vial. Add another 5 mL of 200 mM EDTA (pH 6.0) and stir overnight. Repeat the extraction (steps D6–D8) once more. Transfer the final organic layer to a pre‑weighed 20 mL vial and evaporate solvents overnight on a 37 °C heat block (or in a speed‑vac). Dry the resulting lecithin overnight in a speed‑vac to remove residual moisture. Verify metal removal by adding 75 mM lecithin (24.1 mg) to 500 µL pentane + 13.5 µL water, titrating 1‑hexanol in 50 mM increments (3.125 µL of 8 M 1‑hexanol) until the solution is clear, then acquiring a ¹³¹P 1D NMR spectrum (trimethyl phosphate as standard) to confirm seven sharp peaks.

steps.title: Form DLPC:DPC reverse micelles
steps.instruction: The night before, place DLPC and DPC in a speed‑vac to remove moisture. Weigh 11.6 mg DLPC and 6.6 mg DPC into a 1.5 mL glass vial. Add 500 µL pentane and vortex. Add 12.5 µL of 8 M 1‑hexanol (200 mM final) and vortex until most solids dissolve. Add the calculated water volume (e.g., 13.5 µL for W₀ = 20) together with protein (either directly from the spin concentrator or from the lyophilized buffer). Vortex to mix protein. Then add the surfactant‑pentane mixture to the protein vial and vortex. Titrate additional 1‑hexanol in 200 mM increments (12.5 µL of 8 M 1‑hexanol) until a total of 800 mM 1‑hexanol is reached, vortexing after each addition. Continue titrating in 50 mM increments (3.125 µL of 8 M 1‑hexanol) until the solution becomes visually clear, then add one final 50 mM increment. Pause point: once clear, the RM is stable for months; store at room temperature on a thermomixer or refrigerate if longer storage is needed.

steps.title: Form lecithin:DPC reverse micelles
steps.instruction: The night before, dry lecithin and DPC in a speed‑vac. For a 50:50 ratio, weigh 12.1 mg lecithin and 6.6 mg DPC into a 1.5 mL glass vial (for a 70:30 ratio, use 16.9 mg lecithin and 3.95 mg DPC). Add 500 µL pentane and vortex. Add 3.125 µL of 8 M 1‑hexanol (50 mM) and vortex until most solids dissolve. Add the calculated water volume (e.g., 13.5 µL) and protein as described above, vortexing to solubilize protein. Add the surfactant‑pentane mixture to the protein vial and vortex. Titrate additional 1‑hexanol in 50 mM increments (3.125 µL of 8 M 1‑hexanol) with vortexing after each addition until the solution is clear, then add one more 50 mM increment. Typical total 1‑hexanol required: 400–700 mM. If protein was added from a lyophilized or vacuum‑concentrated sample, transfer the mixture twice (into the surfactant vial and back) after the first and second 1‑hexanol additions to ensure complete solubilization.

steps.title: Form PBL:DPC (or BHL:DPC) reverse micelles
steps.instruction: The night before, dry DPC (and optionally PBL) in a speed‑vac. Weigh 6.6 mg DPC into a 1.5 mL glass vial. Prepare a 100 mg·mL⁻¹ stock of PBL in pentane; for a 50:50 ratio use 112 µL of this stock (22.5 mg·mL⁻¹). Add 388 µL pentane to the DPC vial, vortex, then add 112 µL PBL/pentane solution and vortex. Add 3.125 µL of 8 M 1‑hexanol (50 mM) and vortex until most solids dissolve. Add the calculated water volume and protein (directly from spin concentrator or from lyophilized buffer) and vortex. Transfer the surfactant‑pentane mixture to the protein vial and vortex. Titrate additional 1‑hexanol in 50 mM increments (3.125 µL of 8 M 1‑hexanol) with vortexing until the solution is clear, then add a final 50 mM increment. If protein was added from a lyophilized sample, perform the double‑transfer step after the first and second 1‑hexanol additions. Optionally, add the PBL stock to the glass vial the night before, dry under nitrogen and a speed‑vac, then add DPC directly before adding pentane (skip step G4).

steps.title: Add deuterated lock solvent and load NMR tube
steps.instruction: Add 10 % (v/v) deuterated solvent as a lock; for pentane‑based RMs add 50 µL d‑pentane (or d‑hexane). Transfer the complete RM sample into an NMR tube, seal with Teflon tape (or use a screw‑top tube such as Norell C‑S‑5‑600‑SC‑7) to minimize evaporation.

steps.title: Acquire NMR experiments
steps.instruction: Run standard Bruker pulse sequences. Use echo‑anti‑echo gradient‑selected experiments to suppress surfactant/lipid signals; water‑flip‑back suppression can be turned off. Calibrate pulse length and water frequency as for aqueous samples. Collect a ¹⁵N‑HSQC to confirm encapsulation and monitor sample stability (first increment can be repeated over days).

steps.title: Perform DLS measurements
steps.instruction: Place 500 µL of the RM (use hexane as the carrier solvent) into a quartz cuvette at room temperature. Use a viscosity of 0.356 cP, dielectric constant 2.10, and refractive index 1.38 (hexane/hexanol 0.875 volume ratio for 1 M hexanol in hexane). Measure size on a Malvern Zetasizer Nano with standard DLS settings, recording triplicate measurements to calculate mean diameter and error (e.g., 6.8 nm ± 1.4 nm for GPx4 in a 75 mM lecithin:DPC RM, W₀ = 20).

description: Validation of protocol The protocol described here has been used and validated in: Walters et al. [4]. Investigating protein-membrane interactions using native reverse micelles constructed from naturally sourced lipids. Protein Science (Figure 2, panels a–f) (Figure 4, panels a, d) (Figure 5, panels c, f, i) (Supplementary Figure 2, panels a–e). Labrecque et al. [5]. Membrane-Mimicking Reverse Micelles for High-Resolution Interfacial Study of Proteins and Membranes. Langmuir (Figure 4, panels a–b) (Supplementary Figure 2, panel a). Successful encapsulation of GPx4, along with other proteins, is shown in Walters et al. [4] and Labrecque et al. [5] for all RM systems described here. The confirmation of encapsulation was determined via protein NMR and the validity of the compositions was confirmed through comparable chemical shift perturbation (CSP) in the active and binding sites of the proteins. Ubiquitin was used as a control protein, and NMR revealed that the formulations of the reverse micelles did not impact the aqueous structure of ubiquitin. DLS confirms the formation of uniformly sized RMs, which increase in diameter as the water loading is increased, as expected.
